summary: Same blue-flame 1D fire with a matching black-blue-cyan-white heat ramp and the same decay law, but the port ships far too little cooling by default (whole strip blazes cyan, mean 180 vs 94), runs its flames ~2.2x too fast at 20 fps because it is time-based where the original is frame-stepped, never reproduces the original's authentic 32.80 s freeze that occupies 37.5% of every 87.35 s cycle, and adds three sliders the original does not have.
observations: Both sides are the same 1D fire on the 60 px strip: sparks appear at the low pixel indices (strip base) and heat propagates toward px59 while cooling, drawn on the waterfall as parallel diagonal streaks running in the same direction (left/early -> right/later). Palette family matches: white/pale-cyan at the base, through cyan, to deep blue, and (on the original) to black at the far end.

REFERENCE CYCLE (now treated as authentic per the 2026-08-29 oracle finding on 16.16 wrap): over a 400 s / 20 fps run the ORIGINAL freezes byte-identically four times - onsets 54.55, 141.90, 229.25, 316.65 s, each lasting exactly 32.80 s. Period 87.35 s (54.55 s alive + 32.80 s frozen), i.e. the reference is a still image 37.5% of the time. Dumps confirm true byte-identity: the original's frame at t=55, 60, 70, 80, 86 and 87 s all hash to 12262b31 and it resumes at t=88 s. During the freeze the held frame is a set of static vertical stripes at mean brightness 95.0 - the same mean as its alive stretch (95.7), so the freeze is a motion event, not a brightness event.

THE PORT NEVER FREEZES. zeroMotionFrames = 1 of 8000 over the same 400 s window (the mandatory t=0 frame), and 1 of 4000 at every other configuration tried, including with the sliders dialed to match the original's look. Over the freeze window the port's dumped frames all differ (t=55/60/70/80/86/87 hash bbe1ca42 / e8907270 / d76693cc / cb8e1368 / 165baa6d / fc231551). A viewer watching an evening sees the original stop dead for half a minute every ~87 s while the port burns continuously - the single largest behavioural difference between the two.

The freeze is deterministic and seed-independent: identical onsets and durations at seeds 1, 7 and 1234 (54.55-87.30 and 141.90-174.65 s in each 200 s run). Its DURATION is time-based - exactly 32.80 s at 10, 20 and 40 fps - while the alive interval before it varies with fps (40.90 s at 10 fps, 54.55 s at 20 fps, 163.72 s at 40 fps). The port shows no freeze at any of those rates.

COOLING IS TOO WEAK AT THE PORT'S DEFAULTS. Mean RGB per pixel over t=30-33 s (both sides alive): original px0/10/20/30/40/50/59 luminance 122/161/128/96/60/28/7 - the top third of the strip is essentially black. Port: 206/215/195/175/157/137/119 - never dark. Exact mean RGB at px59: orig R0 G0 B20, port R0 G114 B245 (bright azure). Whole-run means over 400 s: orig meanBrightness 94.2 (R 15.5 / G 82.6 / B 184.7); port 180.5 (R 61.2 / G 225.9 / B 254.4), with meanB pinned at 255 most of the time.

The cooling MODEL and palette are right - only the constant is wrong. Sweeping sliderCooling and comparing the 3 s mean per-pixel RGB profile against the original gives MAE-per-channel 158.4 (0), 86.7 (0.02), 51.4 (0.03), 7.2 (0.045), 28.3 (0.06), 50.3 (0.08), 70.0 (0.12), 87.5 (0.25), 93.5 (1.0). At sliderCooling=0.045 the port's profile is 159/176/131/93/59/29/10 against the original's 122/161/128/96/60/28/7 - the falloff shape and the R/G/B ramp agree to within a few counts from px20 outward.

The port's untouched default cooling is ~0.022, pinned by dial-matching: rendering with sliderCooling=0.022 reproduces the untouched port render to MAE 0.10 per channel over four dumped frames (0.018 -> 15.84, 0.020 -> 7.90, 0.024 -> 7.23, 0.026 -> 14.28). So the default is about half the value that matches the original.

PROPAGATION IS ~2.2x TOO FAST at the harness default. Measured by whole-strip cross-correlation after removing each side's time-mean profile, over 60 dumped frames at t=30-33 s / 20 fps: original 2.00 px/frame at lag 1-2 frames, settling to 1.75 px/frame at longer lags = 34-40 px/s; port 4.00-4.25 px/frame = 80-85 px/s. Visible as streak slope: the original's trails are steep diagonals, the port's are shallow, nearly horizontal.

The two sides use different TIME MODELS, confirmed by tracking position (not the motion stat) at 10/20/40 fps over the same t=30 s window. ORIGINAL: 2.00 / 2.00 / 2.00 px per FRAME (20 / 40 / 70-80 px/s) - frame-stepped. PORT: 80-85 / 80-85 / 80-85 px/s (8.0 / 4.0 / 2.0 px per frame) - time-based. They coincide only near 40 fps; at the 20 fps default the port is the faster one by 2.2x, and at 10 fps by 4x.

Cooling does not affect speed: at sliderCooling 0.02, 0.045 and 0.08 the port holds 80 px/s while the original holds 40 px/s in the same runs. No dial on the port can bring its speed to the original's at 20 fps.

CONTROL SURFACE MISMATCH: the original exposes NO controls (meta.json orig controls: []). The port adds three sliders - sliderCooling (Cooling), sliderSparking (Sparking), sliderTickMs (TickMs). There is nothing on the original side to dial against, so all dialed comparison is one-sided.

The low-fps survey is misleading on the original in a second way: at 5 fps its freeze starts at 36.2 s and the waterfall collapses to flat vertical stripes for the rest of a 60 s window, which reads as a dead original. Re-checked at 20 fps the original animates normally between freezes, so window placement matters - all alive-regime comparisons above were made at 20 fps inside t=30-33 s and t=100-140 s.
Seed independence: seeds 1, 7 and 1234 give the same character on both sides over 200 s (orig mean 94-108, port 180-182), so none of the above is a one-seed fluke.
Neither side binds sensors (wantsSensors false on both, sensors "off"); no compile or runtime errors on either side in any of the ~35 runs.

dials.name: sliderCooling
dials.origEffect: control absent on the original - it exposes no controls at all, so its effect cannot be cross-checked
dials.portEffect: Live and strongly value-dependent, but violently nonlinear and mis-defaulted. 0 rails the whole strip to flat white (mean 255, motion 0). 0.022 is the untouched default. 0.045 reproduces the original's decay profile almost exactly (profile MAE 7.2/channel, mean 100 vs orig 96). 0.06 already truncates the fire at ~px35, 0.08 at ~px25, and 0.25-1.0 leave the strip essentially dead (mean 3-9). The entire useful range sits below 0.1, and the untouched default sits at the wrong end of it. Does not affect propagation speed.

dials.name: sliderSparking
dials.portEffect: Live, value-dependent and monotonic (measured with sliderCooling pinned at 0.045): 0 = fully black, no sparks at all; 0.05 = mean 11; 0.2 = mean 32; 0.5 = mean 100; 0.8 = mean 132; 1.0 = mean 138. 0.5 is the value that reproduces the original's spark density/brightness in the alive regime.

dials.name: sliderTickMs
dials.portEffect: Effectively value-inert but not side-effect-free. With cooling/sparking pinned, values 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 render BYTE-IDENTICAL to each other; 0 differs only marginally (MAE 1.83/channel). But merely SETTING the control at all jumps propagation from 87 px/s to 273 px/s - 3.1x its own untouched rate and ~7x the original's 33-40 px/s - while mean brightness is unchanged (101 at every value). A dial that cannot be steered yet wrecks the pattern by being touched.

feedback: Roughly double the default cooling. The port's untouched default is sliderCooling ~= 0.022; the value that reproduces the original is ~0.045 (measured by dial-matching and by profile MAE, 7.2 vs 87 per channel). Target the original's measured mean per-pixel luminance profile at px0/10/20/30/40/50/59 = 122/161/128/96/60/28/7 over a 3 s window at 20 fps: the strip's far third must be black most of the time, with flames only occasionally licking into it. The cooling model, the falloff shape and the black->blue->cyan->white ramp are all already correct once cooled - this is a single wrong constant, not a wrong model.

Halve the propagation speed at 20 fps and, more importantly, switch the time model. The original advances its heat array a fixed 2 px per rendered FRAME (20 / 40 / 70-80 px/s at 10 / 20 / 40 fps); the port advances a fixed ~82 px/s regardless of frame rate. They agree only near 40 fps. Match the original's frame-stepped advance rather than retuning the port's per-second constant - that fixes the speed at every rate instead of one.

Reproducing the original's TIME MODEL is also what would restore its freeze cadence, which the port is missing entirely. The original accumulates into a 16.16 value that wraps, and the confirmed-authentic consequence is a byte-identical freeze of exactly 32.80 s (32768 ms) recurring every 87.35 s at 20 fps - 37.5% of the pattern's life is a held still frame. The port runs continuously and never freezes (1 zero-motion frame in 8000). If the port keeps a saturating or delta-clamped accumulator it will never show this; porting the plain wrapping add is what makes the two agree over long windows. If reproducing the wrap is deliberately rejected, say so explicitly - but it is currently an unannounced behavioural difference over more than a third of the runtime.

Drop or fix sliderTickMs. It has no usable value-dependence (0.25/0.5/0.75/1.0 render byte-identically; 0 differs by MAE 1.8), yet touching it at all accelerates the fire from 87 px/s to 273 px/s - about 7x the original. Either wire it to something real (it looks like it wants to be the frame-tick period that sets the 2 px/frame advance) or remove it.

Reconsider the three sliders as a whole: the original exposes no controls, so every one is surface the original does not have. More importantly their DEFAULTS are what a user sees, and those defaults are the wrong pattern - a uniformly lit cyan strip instead of blue flames on a mostly dark strip. Whatever is kept, retune so the UNTOUCHED render matches: sliderCooling ~0.045 and sliderSparking ~0.5 are the measured values that do it.

When re-verifying, do not judge from a short window or a low-fps survey. At 5 fps the original freezes from 36.2 s and reads as dead; at 20 fps it freezes 54.55-87.30 s and again 141.90-174.65 s. Compare alive regimes at 20 fps inside t=30-50 s or t=100-140 s, and compare the freeze cadence over at least 200 s.
